analysis.one_liner: Makes public college tuition-free and cuts student loan rates, paid for by a tax on Wall Street trades.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in May 2015, never received a hearing, committee vote, or floor vote; it died when the Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would give federal grants to states—matched 1-to-1 with state dollars—to eliminate tuition and required fees at public colleges. It would cut interest rates on new federal student loans and let current borrowers refinance to today's rates, expand the work-study program, and simplify the federal aid application. To pay for it, the bill places a small tax on each securities trade—0.5% on stock sales, with lower rates on bonds and derivatives—and refunds that tax to households earning under $50,000 ($75,000 for couples).
analysis.who_benefits: Students at public colleges, who would pay no tuition or required fees; student loan borrowers, who could cut their interest rates; and low-income students, who would get additional aid covering living costs. Adjunct and part-time faculty would gain as states are required to shift instruction toward full-time, tenure-track professors.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Public college students and loan borrowers

how_it_helps.text: Directs federal grants to states to eliminate tuition and required fees at public institutions of higher education, with each state matching the federal dollars one-to-one.

Lets federal student loan borrowers modify the interest rate on their existing loans to the current rate at any time during the life of the loan, and lowers rates on new loans issued after July 1, 2015.

Requires states that accept grants to cover the full remaining cost of attendance for Pell Grant recipients after grants and expected family contributions, and to ensure at least 75% of instruction is delivered by tenured or tenure-track faculty within five years.
Expands the Federal Work-Study program from roughly $975 million to $3 billion per year by 2020 and reallocates funds based on the number of low- and moderate-income students a college serves.
Simplifies financial aid by letting students in five pilot states file a single aid application for their whole degree program and using tax data from two years earlier to determine eligibility.
Pays for the program with a 0.5% tax on stock trades and lower rates on bonds and derivatives, and refunds the tax in full to households making under $50,000 ($75,000 for joint filers).

analysis.who_pays: Large financial institutions and frequent traders, who would pay the tax on each securities transaction. The tax is levied on every covered trade, but households under the income thresholds get every dollar of it back, so the net burden falls on higher-income households and institutional traders.

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes $47 billion in new federal spending for fiscal 2016 plus 'such sums as may be necessary' through 2025, a large open-ended commitment on top of required state matching funds.

A transaction tax raises the cost of every trade, and critics argue costs can be passed through to pension funds and ordinary investors and that high-frequency trading could move overseas; the bill includes anti-avoidance rules and whistleblower provisions to counter that.

States would have to commit matching funds and maintain instruction spending, need-based aid, and faculty tenure levels as conditions of the grant—requirements some states could not or would not meet.
Eliminating tuition benefits middle- and upper-income families as well as low-income students, rather than targeting the money only where need is greatest.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For families facing tuition and graduates carrying high-rate loans, the benefits are large and direct. The cost is real but narrowly concentrated: a half-cent-per-dollar tax on trades, with the burden falling almost entirely above the income thresholds where the full credit phases out. The open-ended federal price tag, the state matching burden, and the risk that trading migrates to avoid the tax are the honest costs, and the bill died before any of them could be debated in committee.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee on its first day, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Bernie Sanders introduced the bill alone, with no cosponsors from either party.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance on May 19, 2015.
The committee never held a markup or vote, and the bill never reached the Senate floor; it died when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wall Street trading firms avoided the proposed tax on their transactions, and existing student borrowers kept the interest rates they had. No student received tuition relief, since the bill never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Financial firms that would have paid the trade tax

for.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
for.role: U.S. Senator from Vermont; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Finance Committee as its sole sponsor.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill during the entire Congress.

against.name: Sen. Orrin Hatch
against.what_they_did: As chairman, never brought the bill before the committee for consideration.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so party positions were never tested on the record; the bill had zero cosponsors from either party.

industries.note: The bill taxes every covered securities trade—0.5% on stocks, lower rates on bonds and derivatives—and returns the revenue to households under the income thresholds, so the net cost falls on high-volume traders and institutions. Industry groups widely opposed financial transaction taxes, arguing trading would migrate offshore.

industries.industry: Student loan servicers and loan investors
industries.note: The bill cuts statutory interest rates on new federal loans and lets existing borrowers refinance, reducing interest collected on federal loans and on some guaranteed loans. Servicers of guaranteed loans would see less activity as borrowers moved rates lower.

industries.industry: Contingent (adjunct) faculty and universities' administrative operations
industries.note: States accepting grants must reach 75% tenure-track instruction within five years and are barred from using funds for administrator salaries or stadiums, shifting money toward full-time teaching jobs and away from administrative spending. Adjuncts gain from required compensation and full-time conversion; universities lose flexibility.
